questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the correct preposition to fill in the blank:
The novel has been translated ________ twenty languages.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) into
Why: One translates "from" one language "into" another.
Why not the others: (A) is common in speech, but "into" is the standard form. (B) and (D) are not used with "translate".
Key point: Translate from Hindi into English.

questions.question:
Choose the word most opposite in meaning to the word in capitals:
The chief guest's speech was BRIEF and to the point.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Lengthy
Why: Brief means short; lengthy means long.
Why not the others: (B) and (D) describe a speech but are not opposites. (C) is a synonym.
Key point: Brief and to the point = short and relevant.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
The story was so ________ that the whole class laughed.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) humorous
Why: After "so", an adjective is needed; "humorous" means funny. Note that "humour" drops its "u" in "humorous".
Why not the others: (A) is a noun. (B) means without humour, the opposite. (C) is an adverb.
Key point: Humour, but humorous.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Sentence Transformation and Correctness
questions.question:
Choose the option that best expresses the sentence in indirect speech:
She asked me, "Are you coming tomorrow?"
options: A) She asked me if I was coming the next day.
B) She asked me if I am coming tomorrow.
C) She asked me was I coming the next day.
D) She told me that I was coming tomorrow.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) She asked me if I was coming the next day.
Why: A yes/no question is reported with "if/whether"; "are you coming" becomes "I was coming", and "tomorrow" becomes "the next day".
Why not the others: (B) keeps the present tense and "tomorrow". (C) keeps question order. (D) turns the question into a statement.
Key point: Change tense, pronoun and time word together.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
The children ________ turns on the swing so that nobody was left out.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) took
Why: The fixed collocation is "take turns".
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) do not go with "turns".
Key point: Take turns, take part, take place.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
Call me ________ you reach the hostel.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) as soon as
Why: "As soon as" means "immediately when".
Why not the others: (A) means up to the time, which does not fit "call me". (B) means "if not". (C) shows contrast.
Key point: As soon as = the moment that.

questions.question:
Rearrange the following sentences to form a coherent paragraph:
A. A lighthouse stands on a rocky coast or an island to warn ships of danger.
B. Each lighthouse flashes in its own pattern, so sailors can tell which one they are seeing.
C. Knowing this, they can work out their position and steer clear of the rocks.
D. At night, a powerful lamp at the top sends out a beam that can be seen far out at sea.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) A, D, B, C
Why: A introduces the lighthouse; D describes its beam at night; B explains the flash patterns; C follows with "Knowing this", meaning which lighthouse they see.
Why not the others: (B) explains the pattern before the beam is introduced. (C) begins in the middle. (D) puts "Knowing this" before the information it refers to.
Key point: "Knowing this" points back to the sentence just before.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate phrasal verb to fill in the blank:
There is no milk left, so we will have to ________ it this morning.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) do without
Why: "Do without" means to manage without something.
Why not the others: (B) means to fasten or to decorate. (C) means to abolish. (D) means to do again.
Key point: Do without = manage without.

questions.question:
Rearrange the following parts to complete the sentence that begins: "The scientists discovered that"
A. could survive
B. the bacteria
C. for several days
D. without any oxygen
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) B, A, D, C
Why: "The scientists discovered that the bacteria (B) could survive (A) without any oxygen (D) for several days (C)." The subject must come before its verb.
Why not the others: (A) puts the verb before the subject. (C) begins with a time phrase and leaves "could survive" at the end. (D) begins with the verb and puts the subject after the time phrase.
Key point: Find the subject and the verb of the "that" clause first.

questions.sub_topic: Prepositions in sentences: addicted, boast, persist, acquainted
questions.question:
Match the sentences in List-I with the prepositions in List-II that fill their blanks:

List-I
(A) Many teenagers are addicted ____ their phones.
(B) He likes to boast ____ his wealth.
(C) If you persist ____ breaking the rules, you will be punished.
(D) Are you acquainted ____ the new teacher?

List-II
(I) in
(II) with
(III) of
(IV) to
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Why: Addicted to (IV), boast of (III), persist in (I) and acquainted with (II) are fixed combinations.
Why not the others: (A) swaps "to" and "of"; (B) swaps "of" and "in"; (C) swaps "in" and "with".
Key point: Learn verbs and adjectives together with their prepositions.

questions.question: Choose the word most similar in meaning to INNOCUOUS:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Harmless
Why: Innocuous means not harmful or offensive: an innocuous remark.
Why not the others: (A) is related in origin but refers to guilt. (C) is the opposite. (D) is unrelated.
Key point: An innocuous question causes no offence.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
Wheat, rice and maize are the main ________ crops of India.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) cereal
Why: A "cereal" is a grain crop such as wheat or rice.
Why not the others: (B) A serial is a story told in parts. (C) is a wrong possessive form. (D) means strange and dreamlike.
Key point: Cereal grows in fields; a serial runs on television.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Sentence Transformation and Correctness
questions.sub_topic: Passive voice, present continuous with a name
questions.question:
Choose the option that best expresses the sentence in the passive voice:
Ravi is writing a letter to his uncle.
options: A) A letter was being written by Ravi to his uncle.
B) A letter is written by Ravi to his uncle.
C) A letter is being written by Ravi to his uncle.
D) A letter has been written by Ravi to his uncle.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) A letter is being written by Ravi to his uncle.
Why: The present continuous "is writing" becomes "is being written".
Why not the others: (A) is in the past continuous. (B) is in the simple present. (D) is in the present perfect.
Key point: Continuous tenses use "being" in the passive.

questions.question: Choose the word most similar in meaning to COMMENCE:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Begin
Why: Commence means to begin or start.
Why not the others: (B) and (D) only look similar. (C) is the opposite.
Key point: The examination will commence at nine.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
After the long walk, she went to her room to ________ down for an hour.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) lie
Why: "Lie (down)" means to rest in a flat position; it takes no object. After "to", the base form "lie" is needed.
Why not the others: (A) "Lay" means to put something down and needs an object ("lay the book on the table"). (C) is the past of "lay". (D) is the past participle of "lie" and cannot follow "to".
Key point: You lie down; you lay something down.

questions.question:
Choose the word most similar in meaning to the word in capitals:
The villagers were warned about a FEROCIOUS leopard near the forest.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Fierce
Why: Ferocious means savagely fierce and violent.
Why not the others: (A) describes the villagers, not the leopard. (B) and (C) are unrelated in meaning.
Key point: A ferocious animal is dangerous.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the correctly spelt word to fill in the blank:
The ________ will meet on Friday to choose the new captain.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) committee
Why: The correct spelling has double "m", double "t" and double "e": committee.
Why not the others: (A) has one "t". (B) has one "m". (C) misses the final "e".
Key point: Committee — three double letters.

questions.question:
Select the words that describe "a person who lives alone and avoids other people":
A. hermit
B. heretic
C. recluse
D. renegade
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) A, B and C only
D) A, C and D only
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) A and C only
Why: A "hermit" and a "recluse" both live apart from society.
Why not the others: B (heretic) holds beliefs against accepted religious teaching. D (renegade) deserts a group or cause. Options (A), (C) and (D) include one of them.
Key point: A recluse avoids company; a renegade betrays it.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
The captain's speech raised the ________ of the tired team.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) morale
Why: "Morale" means confidence and enthusiasm, especially of a group.
Why not the others: (A) A moral is a lesson or a principle. (B) means subject to death. (D) means principles of right and wrong.
Key point: The moral of a story; the morale of a team.

questions.sub_topic: Antonym pairs: maximum, arrival, hide, superior
questions.question:
Select the correct pairs of antonyms:
A. maximum — minimum
B. arrival — departure
C. hide — conceal
D. superior — inferior
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: B) B, C and D only
C) A, B and D only
D) A, B, C and D
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) A, B and D only
Why: Maximum and minimum, arrival and departure, superior and inferior are opposites.
Why not the others: Pair C is a pair of synonyms — hide means conceal. Options (A), (B) and (D) include pair C.
Key point: Test each pair on its own.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Sentence Transformation and Correctness
questions.sub_topic: Correct sentences: I were, will see, carefully, since we met
questions.question:
Which of the following sentences are grammatically correct?
A. I wish I were a bird.
B. If I will see him, I will tell him.
C. He drives very careful.
D. Ten years have passed since we last met.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) A, B and C only
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) A and D only
Why: A correctly uses "were" for an imaginary wish. D correctly uses the present perfect with "since".
Why not the others: B should be "If I see him" (no "will" in an "if" clause about the future). C should be "carefully" (an adverb describes "drives"). Options (A), (B) and (C) include B or C.
Key point: In a first conditional, the "if" clause takes the simple present.

questions.question:
Match the figures of speech in List-I with the examples in List-II:

List-I
(A) Metaphor
(B) Alliteration
(C) Irony
(D) Synecdoche

List-II
(I) The farmer has ten mouths to feed.
(II) The dentist had the worst teeth in town.
(III) His words were daggers in her heart.
(IV) Mighty mountains met the morning mist.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Why: Words called daggers — metaphor (III); repeated "m" sounds — alliteration (IV); a dentist with bad teeth — irony (II); "mouths" stands for people — synecdoche (I).
Why not the others: (A) swaps metaphor and alliteration; (B) swaps alliteration and irony; (D) swaps the last two.
Key point: In synecdoche, a part stands for the whole.

questions.question:
Rearrange the following parts to form a meaningful sentence:
A. but he is also
B. a good painter
C. Not only is he
D. an excellent singer
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) C, B, A, D
Why: "Not only is he (C) a good painter (B), but he is also (A) an excellent singer (D)." "Not only" at the start is followed by inversion ("is he").
Why not the others: (A) gives "Not only is he but he is also". (B) and (D) start with a lower-case part.
Key point: Not only + auxiliary + subject, but ... also.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the correct preposition to fill in the blank:
The basket was full ________ ripe mangoes.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) of
Why: The standard expression is "full of".
Why not the others: (A) is used with "filled", not "full". (C) and (D) are wrong.
Key point: Full of; filled with.

questions.question:
Rearrange the following parts to form a meaningful sentence:
A. the climbers continued
B. towards the summit
C. tired after the long night,
D. Although
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) D, C, A, B
Why: "Although (D) tired after the long night (C), the climbers continued (A) towards the summit (B)."
Why not the others: (A) gives "Although the climbers continued tired after the long night, towards the summit". (B) and (C) start with a lower-case part.
Key point: "Although" + its clause, then the main clause.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
His ________ wedding, with three bands and a fleet of imported cars, was criticised in the newspapers.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ostentatious
Why: "Ostentatious" means showy and designed to impress others.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) all suggest modesty or simplicity, which contradicts three bands and imported cars.
Key point: The details (bands, imported cars) point to showiness.

questions.question:
Match the words in List-I with their definitions in List-II:

List-I
(A) Cartographer
(B) Botanist
(C) Sculptor
(D) Archaeologist

List-II
(I) A person who draws maps
(II) A person who studies plants
(III) An artist who carves or shapes stone, wood or metal
(IV) A person who studies the past by digging up ancient remains
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(I), (B)-(II), (C)-(III), (D)-(IV)
Why: Cartographer — map-maker (I); botanist — student of plants (II); sculptor — carver of statues (III); archaeologist — digger of the past (IV).
Why not the others: (B) swaps the first two; (C) swaps the middle two; (D) swaps the last two.
Key point: "Archae-" means ancient.

questions.question: Choose the word most opposite in meaning to ABSURD:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Sensible
Why: Absurd means wildly unreasonable or silly; sensible means reasonable.
Why not the others: (A) and (D) are close in meaning. (B) only looks similar.
Key point: An absurd idea makes no sense.

questions.question:
Rearrange the following parts to form a meaningful sentence:
A. Before the monsoon, farmers
B. their fields
C. for sowing
D. plough
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) A, D, B, C
Why: The opener with the subject (A) is followed by the verb (D), the object (B) and the purpose (C).
Why not the others: (B) and (D) start with a lower-case part. (C) puts the object before the verb.
Key point: Subject, verb, object, purpose.

questions.sub_topic: Idioms: thin ice, read between the lines, ball in your court, sit on the fence
questions.question:
Match the idioms in List-I with their meanings in List-II:

List-I
(A) On thin ice
(B) To read between the lines
(C) The ball is in your court
(D) To sit on the fence

List-II
(I) To find a hidden meaning
(II) It is your turn to act or decide
(III) In a risky situation
(IV) To avoid taking sides
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(II), (D)-(IV)
Why: On thin ice — in a risky position (III); read between the lines — find the hidden meaning (I); the ball is in your court — it is your move (II); sit on the fence — stay neutral (IV).
Why not the others: (A) swaps the first two; (B) swaps the middle two; (C) swaps the last two.
Key point: Learn idioms as whole units of meaning.

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
The ________ number of tigers in the forest alarmed the wildlife officers.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) dwindling
Why: "Dwindling" means gradually becoming smaller, which explains why the officers were alarmed.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) would not alarm wildlife officers.
Key point: "Alarmed" signals bad news.

questions.question:
Match the phrasal verbs in List-I with their meanings in List-II:

List-I
(A) Hold on
(B) Hold up
(C) Hold back
(D) Hold out

List-II
(I) Delay
(II) Wait for a short time
(III) Last, or continue to resist
(IV) Stop oneself from showing or doing something
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(III)
Why: "Hold on, please" — wait (II); traffic held us up — delayed (I); she held back her tears — restrained (IV); the water supply held out — lasted (III).
Why not the others: (A) swaps the first two; (C) swaps hold up and hold back; (D) swaps the last two.
Key point: The particle changes the meaning of "hold".

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
Soldiers are trained in strict ________ to orders.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) obedience
Why: After "strict", a noun is needed: "strict obedience to orders".
Why not the others: (B) is an adjective. (C) is a verb. (D) is an adverb.
Key point: Obey (verb), obedient (adjective), obedience (noun).

questions.topic: Verbal Ability: Choosing the Correct Word
questions.question:
Choose the most appropriate word to fill in the blank:
Let us walk to the market ________ taking an auto.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) instead of
Why: "Instead of" means "in place of": walking replaces taking an auto.
Why not the others: (A) gives a reason. (B) shows contrast. (D) means as a precaution against.
Key point: Instead of + noun or -ing.

questions.question: Choose the one word for: "A person who offers to do work without being paid"
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Volunteer
Why: A volunteer works freely, without payment.
Why not the others: (A) works only for money, often as a soldier. (B) is paid by an employer. (C) is learning a trade, often for low pay.
Key point: Volunteer comes from the Latin for "willing".

questions.sub_topic: What bees come to flowers for
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

A honeybee visiting a flower is not thinking about fruit or seeds. It has come for food: sweet nectar, which it turns into honey, and protein-rich pollen, which it carries home to feed the young bees. But as the bee pushes into the flower, fine grains of pollen stick to the dense hairs on its body. When it visits the next flower of the same kind, some of those grains rub off on to the flower's female parts. This transfer of pollen is called pollination, and without it many plants cannot form fruits or seeds.

Bees are especially good pollinators because they are loyal. On a single trip, a bee usually visits flowers of only one kind, so the pollen it carries reaches the right plants. Bees also share information. A worker that has found a rich patch of flowers performs a "waggle dance" on the honeycomb, and the angle and length of the dance tell the other bees the direction and distance of the food.

The value of this work is enormous. Roughly three out of four of the world's leading food crops, including many fruits, vegetables, nuts and oilseeds, depend at least partly on animal pollinators, and bees are the most important of them. In India, farmers growing mustard, sunflower, apples and litchis often keep beehives near their fields, because better pollination can mean a much larger harvest.

Yet bees face growing dangers. Some pesticides harm them, the loss of wild flowering plants leaves them short of food, and diseases and parasites weaken their colonies. Protecting bees is not only about saving honey; it is about protecting the food on our plates.

Question: According to the passage, why does a honeybee visit a flower?
options: A) To pollinate the plant on purpose
B) To collect nectar and pollen for food
C) To lay its eggs inside the petals
D) To perform its waggle dance there
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) To collect nectar and pollen for food
Why: "It has come for food: sweet nectar, which it turns into honey, and protein-rich pollen." Pollination happens by accident.
Why not the others: (A) The bee "is not thinking about fruit or seeds". (C) is not stated. (D) The dance is performed on the honeycomb.
Key point: Distinguish the bee's purpose from the result of its visit.

Question: Why, according to the passage, are bees especially good pollinators?
options: A) They fly faster than any other insect
B) They avoid flowers that have little nectar
C) They visit flowers only in the morning
D) They usually visit flowers of one kind on a trip
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) They usually visit flowers of one kind on a trip
Why: "On a single trip, a bee usually visits flowers of only one kind, so the pollen it carries reaches the right plants."
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) are not stated.
Key point: "Because" in the question matches the reason given in the passage.

Question: The writer calls bees "loyal". In this context, the word means that bees:
options: A) Keep returning to flowers of the same kind
B) Never leave their own hive for long
C) Always obey the queen of the colony
D) Defend the beekeeper against enemies
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Keep returning to flowers of the same kind
Why: The next sentence explains: a bee "usually visits flowers of only one kind" on a trip.
Why not the others: (B), (C) and (D) are ideas of loyalty not used in the passage.
Key point: Writers often explain an unusual use of a word in the next sentence.

Question: What information does the waggle dance give to other bees?
options: A) The number of flowers in a patch
B) The kind of honey that will be made
C) The direction and distance of the food
D) The danger from pesticides in the area
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The direction and distance of the food
Why: "The angle and length of the dance tell the other bees the direction and distance of the food."

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

A honeybee visiting a flower is not thinking about fruit or seeds. It has come for food: sweet nectar, which it turns into honey, and protein-rich pollen, which it carries home to feed the young bees. But as the bee pushes into the flower, fine grains of pollen stick to the dense hairs on its body. When it visits the next flower of the same kind, some of those grains rub off on to the flower's female parts. This transfer of pollen is called pollination, and without it many plants cannot form fruits or seeds.

Bees are especially good pollinators because they are loyal. On a single trip, a bee usually visits flowers of only one kind, so the pollen it carries reaches the right plants. Bees also share information. A worker that has found a rich patch of flowers performs a "waggle dance" on the honeycomb, and the angle and length of the dance tell the other bees the direction and distance of the food.

The value of this work is enormous. Roughly three out of four of the world's leading food crops, including many fruits, vegetables, nuts and oilseeds, depend at least partly on animal pollinators, and bees are the most important of them. In India, farmers growing mustard, sunflower, apples and litchis often keep beehives near their fields, because better pollination can mean a much larger harvest.

Yet bees face growing dangers. Some pesticides harm them, the loss of wild flowering plants leaves them short of food, and diseases and parasites weaken their colonies. Protecting bees is not only about saving honey; it is about protecting the food on our plates.

Question: "Protecting bees is not only about saving honey; it is about protecting the food on our plates." What does this sentence suggest?
options: A) Honey is the most important food that bees provide
B) The loss of bees would threaten many food crops
C) People should stop eating honey to save bees
D) Bees are more important than all other animals
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The loss of bees would threaten many food crops
Why: The passage has shown that most leading food crops depend partly on pollinators, chiefly bees; losing bees would reduce food supplies.
Why not the others: (A) is what the sentence denies. (C) and (D) are not suggested.
Key point: "Not only ... it is about" moves from a narrow view to a wider one.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

The train to Darbhanga left Mumbai at midnight, and by eleven the platform was already full. Ramesh had a reserved berth for the first time in his life. For eight years, ever since he had come to the city to work on building sites, he had travelled home in the general compartment, standing for the first day and sleeping on newspaper by the door on the second.

This time he had saved for months. In his bag were a cotton saree for his mother, a school bag for his nephew, a steel tiffin carrier for his sister-in-law and, wrapped in a shirt, a small radio for his father, who had been asking for one for years.

The berth turned out to be the middle one, and directly below him a young couple with a baby argued all night about whose mother they would visit first. Ramesh did not mind. He lay with his arm over his bag and watched the dark country slide past the window: the lights of small stations, a fire in a field, a temple on a hill.

On the second evening, as the train crossed the Ganga, he went to the door and stood looking at the wide brown water. A boy beside him asked whether he was going home for Chhath. Ramesh nodded. "And you?" The boy shook his head. "I am going to Mumbai," he said, "for work." He was perhaps sixteen.

Ramesh looked at him for a long time. Then he took a paper from his pocket, wrote down the name of a contractor and a telephone number, and gave it to him. "Tell him Ramesh from Madhubani sent you," he said. "And always keep your arm over your bag."

Question: How had Ramesh travelled home in earlier years?
options: A) In a reserved berth in a sleeper coach
B) By bus, because train tickets were too dear
C) In the general compartment, often standing
D) In the guard's van with the luggage
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) In the general compartment, often standing
Why: He had travelled "in the general compartment, standing for the first day and sleeping on newspaper by the door on the second."
Why not the others: (A) This time was the first. (B) and (D) are not stated.
Key point: Detail questions are answered from the exact line.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

The Lighthouse Keeper

He climbs the hundred-and-twenty steps
each evening as the light grows thin,
a lamp in his hand, a key on a string,
and the whole dark ocean waiting to come in.

He trims the wick, he wipes the glass,
he winds the clockwork round and round,
until the great beam wakes and walks
across the water without a sound.

He never sees the ships he saves;
they are only lights that pass, and go,
a cargo boat, a fishing fleet,
names on a list he will never know.

On stormy nights the tower shakes
and the waves come leaping at the door;
he sits and listens to the wind
and keeps the light, as he has before.

And in the morning, grey and spent,
he climbs back down to the empty shore,
puts out his lamp and boils his tea —
one more night, and one night more.

Question: "Until the great beam wakes and walks / across the water without a sound." The figure of speech used here is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Personification
Why: The beam of light is given the human actions of waking and walking — personification.
Why not the others: (A) There is no "like" or "as". (C) There is no exaggeration. (D) "Without a sound" — no sound is imitated.
Key point: Human actions given to non-human things signal personification.

Question: What do the lines "He never sees the ships he saves; / they are only lights that pass, and go" suggest about the keeper's work?
options: A) He is too careless to watch the sea
B) Ships do not need the lighthouse any more
C) He is paid according to the ships he sees
D) His work is important but unseen and unthanked
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) His work is important but unseen and unthanked
Why: He saves ships whose names he "will never know"; his work matters greatly, yet it brings no recognition or thanks.
Why not the others: (A) He works carefully every night. (B) contradicts "the ships he saves". (C) is not suggested.
Key point: A poem may honour quiet, unnoticed work.

Question: What is the effect of the last line, "one more night, and one night more"?
options: A) It shows that the keeper plans to retire soon
B) It shows that the storm will last two more nights
C) It suggests the patient repetition of his duty, night after night
D) It suggests that he has forgotten how many nights have passed
questions.explanation:

Why not the others: (A) and (B) are not suggested. (D) misreads the repetition.
Key point: Repetition at the end of a poem often stresses continuity.
